claim: Pancreatic cancer has the worst prognosis of all common tumors.
source: Pancreatic cancer has the worst prognosis of all common tumors.
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2020 in the Introduction section

claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma has a 5-year survival of 10%.
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has the worst prognosis of all common tumors, with a 5-year survival of 10% (Siegel et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2020

claim: PDAC is expected to become the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths by 2030.
source: With rising incidence, it is expected that PDAC will become the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths by 2030 (Rahib et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rahib et al., 2014

claim: Less than 20% of PDAC patients present with a potentially resectable and curable tumor.
source: A critical factor for this dismal development is the late diagnosis, with less than 20% of patients presenting with a potentially resectable and curable tumor (Kamisawa et al., 2016; Rahib et al., 2016; Bockorny et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kamisawa et al., 2016; Rahib et al., 2016; Bockorny et al., 2022

claim: Earlier cancer diagnosis could increase survival rates by an estimated fivefold.
source: Earlier cancer diagnosis could increase the survival rates by an estimated fivefold, and more reliable and real-time assessment of treatment effects in patients with cancer could improve quality of life and reduce healthcare costs (Ghatnekar et al., 2013; Matsuno et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ghatnekar et al., 2013; Matsuno et al., 2004

claim: There are no credentialed serologic biomarkers with high enough performance to assist in the early detection of PDAC.
source: Unfortunately, there are no credentialed serologic biomarkers with high enough performance to assist in the early detection of PDAC.
evidence: Statement of current state of knowledge in the field

claim: CA19-9 is fraught with poor sensitivity and specificity and is only used for monitoring disease on treatment or after surgical resection.
source: The best-established biomarker for PDAC, carbohydrate antigen 19–9 (CA19-9), is fraught with poor sensitivity and specificity and is only used for monitoring disease on treatment or after surgical resection (Locker et al., 2006; Galli et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Locker et al., 2006; Galli et al., 2013

claim: Extracellular vesicles, including exosomes and microvesicles, are nanosized particles released by most cell types and can be detected in the circulation.
source: Extracellular vesicles (EVs), including exosomes and microvesicles, are nanosized particles released by most cell types and can be detected in the circulation (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2017

claim: EVs play important roles in transmission of oncogenic and inflammatory signals.
source: EVs play important roles in transmission of oncogenic and inflammatory signals (Costa-Silva et al., 2015), communications between cells and their microenvironment (van Niel et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Costa-Silva et al., 2015 and van Niel et al., 2022

claim: ExoDNA, exoRNA and protein profiles highly reflect parental cells.
source: In addition, exoDNA, exoRNA and protein profiles highly reflect parental cells, therefore offering an attractive strategy for diagnosing cancers non-invasively by analyzing EVs in the circulation (Costa-Silva et al., 2015; Melo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Costa-Silva et al., 2015; Melo et al., 2015

claim: Previous studies employed EVs to discover biomarkers for PDAC using cell lines or tumor tissue.
source: Previous studies employed EVs to discover biomarkers for PDAC (Melo et al., 2015; Madhavan et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2017; Castillo et al., 2018); however, those discovery proteomics experiments were carried out using cell lines or tumor tissue, which are not representative of the heterogeneity of human PDAC and are unable to recapitulate the systemic responses to cancer (Madhavan et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2017; Castillo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Melo et al., 2015; Madhavan et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2017; Castillo et al., 2018

claim: The discovery cohort was comprised of 124 individuals, including PDAC (N=93), chronic pancreatitis (N=12), IPMN (N=8) and healthy controls (N=11).
source: The discovery cohort was comprised of 124 individuals, including pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC, N=93), chronic pancreatitis (CP, N=12), intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN, N=8) and healthy controls (N=11).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1

claim: Subjects in the pancreatic cancer group had a mean age of 66.5 years (range, 37–91), and 48.4% were female.
source: Subjects in the pancreatic cancer group (N=93) had a mean age of 66.5 years (range, 37–91), and 48.4% were female.
evidence: Demographic data from the study cohort

claim: All subjects had biopsy-proven disease.
source: All subjects had biopsy-proven disease.
evidence: Description of study inclusion criteria

claim: Thirty subjects had early-stage disease (stages I-II) and 63 had advanced disease (stages III-IV).
source: Thirty subjects had early-stage disease (stages I-II) and 63 had advanced disease (stages III-IV).
evidence: Demographic data from the study cohort

claim: EVtrap is a magnetic bead‐based isolation method that enables highly efficient capture of EVs from biofluids.
source: As described in recent reports, EVtrap is a magnetic bead‐based isolation method that enables highly efficient capture of EVs from biofluids, confirmed by multiple common EV markers (Iliuk et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2018; Nunez Lopez et al., 2022; Hinzman et al., 2022a; Hinzman et al., 2022b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Iliuk et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2018; Nunez Lopez et al., 2022; Hinzman et al., 2022a; Hinzman et al., 2022b

claim: The vast majority of particles isolated by EVtrap had diameters between 100 and 200 nm, consistent with exosomes.
source: Previous analyses using electron microscopy and nanoparticle tracking also confirmed that the vast majority of particles isolated by EVtrap had diameters between 100 and 200 nm, consistent with exosomes (Iliuk et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Iliuk et al., 2020

claim: EVtrap isolates demonstrate higher abundance of CD9, a common exosome marker, as compared to isolates from other traditional EV isolation methods.
source: In addition, EVtrap isolates demonstrates higher abundance of CD9, a common exosome marker, as compared to isolates from other traditional EV isolation methods such as size exclusion chromatography and ultracentrifugation (Iliuk et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Iliuk et al., 2020

claim: Over 95% recovery yield can be achieved by EVtrap with less contamination from soluble proteins.
source: Over 95% recovery yield can be achieved by EVtrap with less contamination from soluble proteins, a significant improvement over current commercially available methods as well as ultracentrifugation (Iliuk et al., 2020; Nunez Lopez et al., 2022; Shuen et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Iliuk et al., 2020; Nunez Lopez et al., 2022; Shuen et al., 2022

claim: Transmission electron microscopy analysis of the EV pellet showed cup-shaped extracellular vesicles.
source: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis of the EV pellet showed cup-shaped extracellular vesicles (exosomes and microvesicles; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: TEM imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Nanoparticle tracking analysis demonstrated that the isolated EVs were in the 100–200 nm diameter range, with a mean diameter of 152 nm.
source: nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) using ZetaView instrument (Particle Metrix) demonstrated that the isolated EVs were in the 100–200 nm diameter range, with a mean diameter of 152 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: NTA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Pearson correlation analysis revealed a very high correlation (r2 >0.97) between technical replicates.
source: the test plasma sample was processed in six replicates and Pearson correlation analysis revealed a very high correlation (r2 >0.97) between replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Correlation analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: In the discovery cohort, 1708 unique proteins were identified.
source: In this cohort, we identified 1708 unique proteins (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Proteomics data from the discovery cohort

claim: The number of unique EV proteins detected per 100 µL of plasma sample varied from 817 to 1128, with an average of 912 unique proteins per sample.
source: The number of unique EV proteins detected per 100 µL of plasma sample varied from 817 to 1128, with an average of 912 unique proteins per sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Proteomics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: No differences were observed between non-tumor and tumor samples regarding the overall number of EV proteins identified.
source: We did not observe differences between non-tumor and tumor samples regarding the overall number of EV proteins identified.
evidence: Analysis of proteomics data from the study

claim: Within the PDAC group, no significant differences were observed in the average number of EV proteins detected for different disease stages.
source: Within the PDAC group, we did not observe significant differences in the average number of EV proteins detected for different disease stages.
evidence: Analysis of proteomics data from the study

claim: A total of 207 proteins were identified that met the criteria for differential expression in pancreatic diseases compared to controls.
source: A total of 207 proteins were identified that met the criteria, with the largest number of differentially expressed markers in PDAC (176), followed by chronic pancreatitis (55) and IPMN (3) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Differential expression analysis from the discovery cohort

claim: Principal component analysis showed control samples as a tight cluster segregated away from PDAC samples but closer to IPMN and chronic pancreatitis patients.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of these markers showed control samples as a tight cluster segregated away from PDAC samples but closer to IPMN and chronic pancreatitis patients (Figure 2A).
evidence: PCA analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: 182 differentially expressed proteins were identified in malignant cases compared to benign pancreatic diseases (92 over-expressed and 90 with reduced expression).
source: We identified 182 differentially expressed proteins in malignant cases (92 over-expressed and 90 with reduced expression; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Differential expression analysis comparing PDAC to benign diseases

claim: Several markers had remarkable overexpression in PDAC (greater than tenfold), including PDCD6IP, SERPINA12, RUVBL2.
source: Several of those markers had remarkable overexpression in PDAC (greater than tenfold), including PDCD6IP, SERPINA12, RUVBL2, among others, as shown in the volcano plot (Figure 2B).
evidence: Differential expression data shown in volcano plot in Figure 2B

claim: Unsupervised clustering showed a clear separation between PDAC and benign pancreatic diseases.
source: Unsupervised clustering showed a clear separation between PDAC and benign pancreatic diseases.
evidence: Clustering analysis of proteomics data

claim: Individuals with IPMN were more closely related to controls, whereas chronic pancreatitis cases were more closely related to PDAC.
source: Individuals with IPMN were more closely related to controls, whereas chronic pancreatitis cases were more related to PDAC (Figure 2C).
evidence: Clustering analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: The PDAC cohort was separated into two subgroups: the first, enriched for early-stage tumors and more closely related to other pancreatic diseases; the second, enriched for advanced and metastatic cases.
source: In addition, the PDAC cohort was separated into two subgroups: the first, enriched for early-stage tumors and more closely related to the other pancreatic diseases (chronic pancreatitis and IPMN); the second, enriched for advanced and metastatic cases with expression profiles further apart from early-stage cancer and pancreatic diseases (Figure 2C).
evidence: Clustering analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: PDCD6IP, SERPINA12, KRT20 showed statistically significant population-wise enrichment in pancreatic cancer compared to benign pancreatic diseases.
source: We further noticed that some proteins such as PDCD6IP, SERPINA12, KRT20 showed statistically significant population-wise enrichment in pancreatic cancer compared to benign pancreatic diseases (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: KRT20 (keratin 20), a gastrointestinal epithelia-associated keratin, was increased in PDAC patient EVs.
source: Interestingly, KRT20 (keratin 20), a gastrointestinal epithelia-associated keratin, was increased in PDAC patient EVs, while keratins associated basal cells, KRT4, KRT15, and KRT3, were reduced.
evidence: Proteomics data from the study

claim: KRT20 overexpression is frequently found in pancreatic tumor tissues and correlates with poor prognosis.
source: KRT20 overexpression is frequently found in pancreatic tumor tissues and correlates with poor prognosis (Schmitz-Winnenthal et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmitz-Winnenthal et al., 2006

claim: 85 proteins were differentially expressed between metastatic and non-metastatic pancreatic cancer.
source: We compared the cEV proteome profiles of individuals with metastatic cancer to those without metastasis and identified 85 proteins differentially expressed between the two groups (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Differential expression analysis comparing metastatic vs non-metastatic PDAC

claim: Supervised clustering between metastatic and non-metastatic diseases showed a clear separation with two distinct expression patterns.
source: Supervised clustering between metastatic and non-metastatic diseases showed a clear separation with two distinct expression patterns (Figure 3A).
evidence: Clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: PSMB4, RUVBL2, and ANKAR EV protein levels were increased in patients with metastatic disease.
source: In particular, PSMB4, RUVBL2, and ANKAR (Figure 3B) EV protein levels were increased in patients with metastatic disease
evidence: Differential expression data shown in Figure 3B

claim: RAP2B, SERPINA12, and IGLV4-69 abundance levels were decreased in the cEVs of patients with metastasis.
source: whereas RAP2B, SERPINA12, and IGLV4-69 abundance levels were decreased in the cEVs of patients with metastasis (Figure 3C).
evidence: Differential expression data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The cEV expression of RALB, CRP, and CD55 had a significant correlation with overall survival.
source: We identified that the cEV expression of RALB, CRP, and CD55 had a significant correlation with overall survival, with a trend for PDCD6IP (Figure 3D).
evidence: Survival analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: A set of seven EV protein signature comprised of RUVBL2, PDCD6IP, ATP5F1, DLD, KRT20, CCT4, and SERPINAI2 gave 100% accuracy when tested in the discovery cohort.
source: We found a set of seven EV protein signature comprised of RUVBL2, PDCD6IP, ATP5F1, DLD, KRT20, CCT4, and SERPINAI2, that gave 100% accuracy when tested in the discovery cohort (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Classification model performance data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and 3

claim: The independent validation cohort consisted of 36 new subjects (24 with PDAC, 6 with chronic pancreatitis, and 6 with IPMN).
source: The independent validation cohort consisted of 36 new subjects (24 with PDAC, 6 with chronic pancreatitis, and 6 with IPMN; Supplementary file 9).
evidence: Description of validation cohort

claim: A total of 10 proteins, including all 7 signature proteins, showed a significant difference (p<0.05) in patients with PDAC as compared to benign pancreatic diseases in the validation cohort.
source: A total of 10 proteins, including all 7 signature proteins, showed a significant difference (p<0.05) in patients with PDAC as compared to benign pancreatic diseases (Figure 4A).
evidence: Validation data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The seven EV protein signature yielded an 89% prediction accuracy in the independent validation cohort.
source: The performance of seven EV protein signature was further tested using SVM model, in our independent validation cohort, yielding an 89% prediction accuracy (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Classification model performance data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: No single marker achieved sufficiently high sensitivity and specificity as the combined model for the diagnosis of pancreatic cancer.
source: As expected, we observed that no single marker achieved sufficiently high sensitivity and specificity as the combined model for the diagnosis of pancreatic cancer.
evidence: Analysis of individual marker performance compared to combined model

claim: PSMB4 (proteasome subunit beta type-4) has been identified as the first proteasomal subunit with oncogenic properties and associated to poor prognosis in several tumors including melanoma, breast, and ovarian cancers.
source: Notably, PSMB4 (proteasome subunit beta type-4), a protein of the ubiquitin-proteasome degradation pathway, has been identified as the first proteasomal subunit with oncogenic properties and associated to poor prognosis in several tumors including melanoma, breast, and ovarian cancers (Liu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2014

claim: PDCD6IP tissue expression in liver metastasis of pancreatic cancer has been found to correlate with improved prognosis in patients with PDAC.
source: In line with our findings, its tissue expression in liver metastasis of pancreatic cancer has been found to also correlate with improved prognosis in patients with PDAC in the study of Law et al., 2020.
evidence: Supported by citation to Law et al., 2020

source: A recent modeling study showed that a new diagnostic assay for PDAC would have to perform with a minimum sensitivity of 88% and a specificity of 85% to reduce healthcare expenditure and prolong survival (Ghatnekar et al., 2013).

source: Serum CA19-9, the best-established blood test for PDAC, has a pooled sensitivity of 75.4% and a specificity of 77.6% (Zhang et al., 2015).
